name: Ambiguity Detection / Proof
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai grammar AMBIGUOUS hai ya nahi, prove karo via parse trees — classic 'dangling-else' style questions is pattern ka signature hain.
whatShouldComeToMind: Find ONE specific string, construct TWO different parse trees (or leftmost derivations) for it — if both succeed differently, ambiguous.
The dangling-else problem (if-then-else nesting) is THE canonical ambiguity example — recognize this shape immediately.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Pick a specific string likely to expose ambiguity (often nested/repeated structure).
2. Attempt TWO different derivation orders/choices that both successfully derive the SAME string.
3. If both succeed with DIFFERENT tree structures, the grammar is ambiguous — exhibit both trees as the proof.
variationsObserved: Comparing an ambiguous grammar to its DISAMBIGUATED version — verify both generate the SAME language despite different ambiguity status.
'Grammar has left AND right recursion' framing — NOT enough info alone to conclude ambiguity, must check directly.
commonTraps: Assuming left+right recursion automatically implies ambiguous — need direct verification.
Testing only ONE derivation attempt and concluding 'unambiguous' — must actively SEARCH for a second differing derivation before concluding unambiguous.

name: Parser-Class Determination (LL(1)/LR(1)/SLR/LALR/conflicts)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai grammar LL(1) hai ya nahi, ya SLR/LALR/LR(1) classify karna hai, ya parsing table me conflicts (shift-reduce/reduce-reduce) find karne hain — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (47 me se 12 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: LL(1): compute FIRST/FOLLOW, check no cell in predictive table has multiple entries.
LR-family: construct LR(0)/LR(1) item sets, check for shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflicts in the resulting automaton.
Left recursion / ambiguity immediately DISQUALIFIES LL(1); ambiguity disqualifies ANY LR(k).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Check for obvious disqualifiers first: left recursion (kills LL(1)), ambiguity (kills BOTH LL(1) and all LR(k)).
2. For LL(1): compute FIRST sets of each production's RHS, FOLLOW sets of relevant non-terminals, check overlap in the predictive table.
3. For LR-family: build the canonical LR(0)/LR(1) item collection (via closure and goto operations), check each state for conflicts.
4. Remember the hierarchy: SLR(1)⊊LALR(1)⊊LR(1) — a grammar failing SLR(1) might still pass LALR(1) or LR(1).
variationsObserved: Partially-filled parsing table given, asked to complete specific cells — apply the table-construction rules to just the missing entries.
'Number of items in a specific item-set I_k' — construct that specific set via closure/goto from the augmented grammar.
commonTraps: Applying SLR's simpler FOLLOW-based conflict resolution when the question actually requires full LR(1) lookahead-based analysis (these can give different conflict verdicts).

name: Grammar Transformation (remove left recursion, ε-productions, CNF conversion)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai grammar se LEFT RECURSION hatao, ya ε-PRODUCTIONS remove karo, ya CNF me convert karo — ye mechanical transformation pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Left recursion removal: A→Aα|β becomes A→βA', A'→αA'|ε (standard formula).
ε-production removal: find all NULLABLE non-terminals first, then for every production containing a nullable non-terminal, add a version WITHOUT it.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For left recursion: identify A→Aα|β pattern, apply the standard rewrite formula directly.
2. For ε-removal: first find ALL nullable non-terminals (those that can derive ε, directly or transitively), then systematically add alternative productions omitting each nullable symbol.
3. For CNF: eliminate ε-productions and unit productions first, then break down long RHS strings into binary (A→BC) chains, and isolate terminals in mixed productions.
variationsObserved: 'Minimum number of production rules' after transformation — verify the transformed grammar isn't just correct but also MINIMAL (no redundant rules).
commonTraps: Missing INDIRECT left recursion (A→Bα, B→Aβ — recursion through another non-terminal, not immediately visible) — must resolve this to direct form first before applying the standard removal formula.

name: Identify the Language Generated by a Grammar
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek grammar di hai aur poocha hai L(G) kya hai, ya ek specific string generate hoti hai ya nahi, ya derivation length kya hogi — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (47 me se 12 PYQs), CFL topic ke Grammar-Language-Identification pattern ka direct overlap.
whatShouldComeToMind: Derive a few short strings by hand from S, look for the emerging pattern.
For 'how many derivation trees for string X' — count DISTINCT valid derivation sequences, watch for ambiguity implications.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Start deriving from S, generate 2-3 short strings.
2. Identify the pattern (matched counts? specific structure?).
3. For derivation-length/count questions, systematically enumerate the specific derivation(s) for the target string.
variationsObserved: Programming-language-style declarations (array dimensions like int a[10][3]) — translate the real-world syntax requirement into grammar rules and verify against given options.
commonTraps: Not checking enough short strings before generalizing the pattern — verify against at least one non-trivial case.

name: Grammar Structural Properties (operator grammar, cycles, CFG expressiveness limits, SDT value computation)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai grammar OPERATOR GRAMMAR rules violate karta hai ya nahi, ya grammar me CYCLES hain ya nahi, ya CFG kis cheez ko express NAHI kar sakta, ya translation-scheme se VALUE compute karni hai — ye broader structural/semantic pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Operator grammar rule: NO ε-productions, and NO two adjacent non-terminals (must have a terminal between any two consecutive non-terminals on RHS).
CFG CANNOT express context-sensitive requirements like 'declare before use' (needs tracking across arbitrary distance, beyond single-stack power) — a classic 'what CFG can't do' fact.
For SDT value computation: evaluate semantic actions bottom-up (or per the scheme's attribute-flow direction) as the parse proceeds.
conceptsRequired: Basic SDT evaluation (cross-link to Syntax Directed Translation topic)
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For operator-grammar checks: scan each production for ε-RHS or adjacent-non-terminal patterns.
2. For 'what can't CFG express' questions: recall that CFG can't enforce SEMANTIC/context-sensitive constraints (variable declared before use, type matching) — only pure syntactic nesting.

3. For SDT/translation-scheme value questions: trace the parse and apply semantic actions in the specified order (usually bottom-up for LR-style, matching each rule's semantic action to its point in the derivation).
variationsObserved: Non-associative operator grammar allowing/disallowing redundant parentheses — check if the grammar's structure permits extra bracketing around already-grouped expressions.
commonTraps: Forgetting BOTH operator-grammar restrictions (no ε AND no adjacent non-terminals) — missing one of the two conditions.
